vignette:
Detective Marcus

Marcus is a twenty-six-year-old detective with the city police department, a position he worked toward deliberately throughout his twenties. He has a sharp mind for detail and an ability to remain composed under pressure—qualities that made him excellent at his job. He's been married to David for three years, and until eighteen months ago, he believed he had built a stable, happy life.

The abuse began subtly. David's criticism of Marcus's work hours escalated into accusations of infidelity. When Marcus tried to discuss boundaries, David would become explosive, throwing objects across their apartment. Marcus found himself apologizing for things he hadn't done, rearranging his schedule to appease David, anything to prevent the next eruption. As a detective trained to read people and situations, Marcus recognizes the pattern now—the cycle of tension, incident, reconciliation—but in the moment, he was caught in a kind of cognitive dissonance. This was his husband. This wasn't supposed to happen to him.

One evening, after Marcus mentioned grabbing drinks with a colleague, David attacked him. The confrontation escalated from shoving to David pinning Marcus against the kitchen counter, landing repeated blows to his ribs and face. Marcus, trained in restraint and de-escalation, did not fight back. He froze. Afterward, David wept and apologized profusely, and Marcus made the decision to leave the next morning.

That was eighteen months ago. Marcus filed for divorce and moved into a small apartment. Externally, he returned to work, to the routines and structures that had always grounded him. Internally, everything fractured.

Now, Marcus sits at his desk at the precinct and finds his hands trembling when he reviews case files involving intimate partner violence. He's hyperaware of every movement his colleagues make around him—a sudden gesture, a raised voice during interrogation, and his body floods with adrenaline. He excuses himself to the bathroom to breathe through the panic. His sergeant has noticed him requesting desk assignments rather than field work, something uncharacteristic for someone who loved the investigative process.

Sleep is nearly impossible. Marcus lies awake replaying the evening, wondering what he could have done differently, whether he somehow provoked it. When he does sleep, he experiences vivid nightmares where he's back in that kitchen, unable to move, unable to call for help. He wakes gasping, drenched in sweat, and often doesn't return to bed.

His wife—he still thinks of David that way sometimes, despite the divorce papers—appears in unexpected places. Marcus will be at the grocery store and see someone with David's build, and his entire nervous system goes into overdrive. He's begun avoiding certain routes, certain establishments, narrowing his world to feel safer. He's stopped attending the gym where he used to find solace, stopped meeting friends for dinner. His apartment has become smaller and smaller.

What troubles Marcus most is the shame. He's a detective. He's trained to recognize danger, to protect himself and others. Yet he was unable to protect himself from someone who claimed to love him. This contradiction plays on repeat in his mind. When colleagues mention their relationships casually, Marcus feels a deep isolation—they wouldn't understand. They might question his competence, wonder if the same man who missed the warning signs in his own home can be trusted to investigate others'.

He hasn't told anyone at work the full truth. He's constructed a narrative about irreconcilable differences, about growing apart. The lie feels necessary for survival, yet it compounds his sense of disconnection from the people around him.
